script.opening: (Hoarse, slow, wrapped in a hoodie; propped up in bed in student halls.) "I've had an awful sore throat for over a week, I'm running temperatures, my neck glands are up and I'm absolutely wiped — I can barely get to lectures. My mate said I need antibiotics. Can you just prescribe some so I can get back to rugby? We've got a big match Saturday."

facts.text: "It kills to swallow, but I'm getting drinks down. Breathing's fine." No drooling, no muffled voice, can open his mouth fully. If asked to show his throat on camera: big tonsils with white patches.
"Here… they're up at the front and down the back of my neck" — points to both sides; tender.
"Way worse. I sleep all afternoon and still feel flattened." Temperatures up to 38.5°C most evenings for 9 days.
"Tummy's fine. No rash. Haven't looked at the roof of my mouth." No yellow skin or dark urine. Eating little.
"Just paracetamol. No allergies." Hasn't been given any antibiotics.
"There are people around at uni." If asked sensitively: a new girlfriend a month ago; no other risks; never had an HIV test.
First-year sports science student, lives in halls. Plays rugby (prop) and lifts weights 4 times a week. "Missing lectures is stressing me out."
Can get to the surgery for a blood test and a tummy check if he gets a lift from a friend.

Fed up and keen to play: "Tonsillitis, I reckon. I just need to be fit for Saturday. It's a big one." Pushes: "So no antibiotics at all? My mate got them." Gutted about rugby: "That's gutting. Could I just play half?" Accepts once the spleen risk is explained clearly. Asks for a note for university.

ice.concerns: Missing the big match and lectures; frustrated at feeling so wiped out.
ice.expectations: "Antibiotics, and back for rugby on Saturday."

cues: "Absolutely wiped." — marked fatigue points beyond simple tonsillitis.
"Big match Saturday." — contact sport and spleen safety.
"My mate said I need antibiotics." — expectation to manage.

checkpoints.text: Recognises INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS (glandular fever, EBV) in a young adult from prolonged sore throat + profound fatigue + fever + (esp. posterior cervical) lymphadenopathy + tonsillar exudate ± splenomegaly/palatal petechiae

Confirms appropriately — monospot/heterophile antibody, FBC (atypical lymphocytes), LFTs — and knows the monospot can be FALSELY NEGATIVE in the first week (repeat / EBV serology), offering an HIV test if negative (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020)
Explains it is VIRAL with SUPPORTIVE management (rest, fluids, analgesia/antipyretics), and resists the antibiotic request with a clear explanation rather than prescribing to satisfy it
AVOIDS amoxicillin/ampicillin (florid maculopapular rash in EBV) — and knows antibiotics are not indicated anyway (penicillin V if a genuine coexisting bacterial tonsillitis needed treating)

Gives the SPLENIC RUPTURE safety advice — avoid contact/collision sports and heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks (NICE CKS) and until reviewed (so no rugby Saturday), arranging a face-to-face spleen check — and warns of sudden severe abdominal/LUQ/shoulder-tip pain
Reads the wish for antibiotics + quick return to sport, explains kindly why both must wait, and checks understanding without leaving him feeling dismissed
Communicates the diagnosis and expected (sometimes prolonged) recovery realistically, supporting a frustrated young patient

Safety-nets and follows up: airway compromise (severe swelling/difficulty swallowing/breathing), splenic rupture (severe abdominal pain), dehydration, prolonged/atypical course (persistent lymphadenopathy/weight loss → re-review), and review — supportive care + sport rule, not antibiotics

worked.txt: "I don’t think antibiotics are the answer here — and I’ll explain why. A really sore throat with weeks of exhaustion, fevers and these neck glands in someone your age is most likely glandular fever, a viral infection. I’ll confirm it with a blood test."

"Because it’s viral, antibiotics won’t touch it — they’d just risk side-effects. In fact one common antibiotic, amoxicillin, gives people with glandular fever a dramatic rash, so we specifically avoid it. The treatment is rest, fluids and painkillers."

"Now, the important one: glandular fever swells the spleen, and a knock — like in rugby — can rarely make it rupture, which is dangerous. So no heavy lifting or strenuous exercise for at least a month, and no contact sport for at least four weeks — longer if your spleen is still enlarged. I’m sorry, but Saturday’s match is out."

"I’ll do a blood test — sometimes it’s negative very early so we may repeat it. Honestly, the tiredness can hang around for a few weeks; pace yourself with lectures. Most people are over the worst in two to four weeks."

"Crucial warning: if you get sudden severe pain in the left upper side of your tummy or your left shoulder tip, that could be the spleen — call 999 / go to A&E. And if your throat swells so much you struggle to swallow or breathe, that’s urgent too."

"Come back if you’re not improving, the glands persist for weeks, or you lose weight — we’d reassess. And we’ll check when it’s safe to get back to rugby rather than guess. I know it’s frustrating — you’ll get there."

f.learning: In a YOUNG ADULT, a prolonged severe SORE THROAT with profound FATIGUE, fever, tender (especially POSTERIOR cervical) LYMPHADENOPATHY, tonsillar enlargement/exudate, and sometimes splenomegaly, hepatitis or palatal petechiae, is INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS (glandular fever), usually EBV — the fatigue and posterior cervical nodes helping distinguish it from simple tonsillitis. Confirm with the MONOSPOT/heterophile antibody test and FBC (atypical lymphocytes), checking LFTs (EBV hepatitis is common), and remember the monospot can be FALSELY NEGATIVE in the first week (repeat or use EBV-specific serology, and offer an HIV test if negative in a mononucleosis-like illness, BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020). Explain it is VIRAL — antibiotics do NOT help and are not indicated — with SUPPORTIVE management (rest, fluids, analgesia/antipyretics, saltwater gargles), resisting the antibiotic request with a clear explanation. A classic pitfall: AVOID AMOXICILLIN/ampicillin, which causes a florid maculopapular RASH in EBV (and is not needed anyway; penicillin V would be used if a genuine coexisting bacterial tonsillitis required treatment). Critically, glandular fever causes SPLENOMEGALY and the spleen can rupture, so advise AVOIDING CONTACT/COLLISION SPORTS and heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks from the start of symptoms and until reviewed (NICE CKS; longer while the spleen is enlarged), checking the spleen face to face — hence no rugby — and warn of sudden severe left-upper-quadrant/abdominal or shoulder-tip pain (splenic rupture, an emergency). The hidden agenda is the wish for antibiotics and a fast return to sport; explain kindly why both must wait, give realistic recovery expectations (fatigue can linger), and safety-net for airway compromise (severe swelling, difficulty swallowing/breathing), splenic rupture, dehydration, and a prolonged/atypical course (persistent lymphadenopathy/weight loss prompting re-review).

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG84 Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2018) · [2] Amoxicillin summary of product characteristics, section 4.4 (avoid if infectious mononucleosis suspected) · [3] Ebell MH et al. JAMA 2016 (diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis) · [4] Sylvester JE et al. Am Fam Physician 2023 (infectious mononucleosis: rapid evidence review) · [5] BHIVA/BASHH/BIA Adult HIV testing guidelines (2020) · [7] NICE NG206 ME/CFS (2021)
knowledge.summary: A young adult with more than a week of severe sore throat, fever, marked fatigue and posterior as well as anterior neck nodes most likely has glandular fever (EBV). Confirm with FBC and film and EBV serology (or a heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, per the local laboratory pathway), with LFTs if clinically indicated. It is viral: antibiotics will not help, and amoxicillin causes a florid rash. The key safety message is the spleen: no contact sport or heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks and until reviewed, so no rugby on Saturday. Safety-net for airway obstruction and splenic rupture.

points.t: Prolonged sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate, marked fatigue, and tender posterior cervical nodes are typical of infectious mononucleosis in teenagers and young adults. Palatal petechiae, splenomegaly and mild hepatitis support it. Ebell (JAMA 2016) [3]: posterior cervical, axillary or inguinal nodes, palatal petechiae and splenomegaly make it more likely.

FBC and film (lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes), and EBV-specific serology as the preferred confirmatory test per the local laboratory pathway; LFTs if jaundice, hepatomegaly or marked systemic illness. A heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, where used, is about 87% sensitive and 91% specific and is unreliable in the first week [3], so a negative result does not exclude EBV when suspicion remains. If negative with a mononucleosis-like illness, offer an HIV test: BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020 [5] lists mononucleosis-like syndrome as an indicator condition.

EBV is viral and antibiotics do not shorten it. Amoxicillin (and ampicillin) cause a widespread maculopapular rash in most people with glandular fever; the SPC [2] advises avoiding it when infectious mononucleosis is suspected. If a separate bacterial tonsillitis needed treating, NICE NG84 [1] first choice is phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 to 10 days (dose per BNF).

Rest as needed, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever (dose per BNF), saltwater gargles. Avoid alcohol while unwell and until liver tests settle. Most people feel better within 2 to 4 weeks, but tiredness can last longer.

Splenic rupture is rare (often quoted as about 0.1 to 0.5%, though exact estimates are uncertain) but potentially fatal; most reported cases occur in the first month, although late rupture can occur [4]. Advise no contact or collision sport and no heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks from the start of symptoms, and longer while the spleen is enlarged or he is unwell. Agree the return at review, not by guesswork.

Airway: drooling, inability to swallow fluids, noisy breathing or breathlessness → emergency. Splenic rupture: sudden severe left upper abdominal pain, left shoulder-tip pain, faintness → 999. Also severe dehydration, jaundice or bleeding.

Persistent or enlarging nodes, night sweats, weight loss or splenomegaly without explanation need reassessment: [6] lymphoma criteria. Fatigue beyond 6 weeks with post-exertional symptoms: consider ME/CFS assessment per NICE NG206 [7].

model.text: Hi Theo, I’m Dr Hughes. What’s been going on?

I’ve had an awful sore throat for over a week, I’m running temperatures, my neck glands are up and I’m absolutely wiped. I can barely get to lectures. My mate said I need antibiotics. Can you just prescribe some so I can get back to rugby? We’ve got a big match Saturday.
That sounds really rough, and I can hear the match matters. Let me ask a few questions and have a look on camera, then we’ll talk about antibiotics and rugby properly. Okay?
model.why: Acknowledges the request and agrees an agenda

model.text: Yeah, go on.
Can you swallow fluids and your own saliva all right? Any drooling, noisy breathing or trouble breathing?
It kills to swallow, but I’m getting drinks down. Breathing’s fine.
Good. Could you open wide and point the camera at your throat, then run your fingers down the sides and back of your neck and show me where the glands are?
model.why: Remote look at the tonsils and node distribution

model.text: Here… they’re up at the front and down the back of my neck.
Your tonsils look big with white patches, and the glands at the back of the neck matter. How tired are you compared to a normal cold?
model.why: Notes posterior nodes and quantifies fatigue

model.text: Way worse. I sleep all afternoon and still feel flattened.
Any pain in your tummy, especially the upper left side, or yellow eyes or skin? Any rashes, or small spots on the roof of your mouth?
Tummy’s fine. No rash. Haven’t looked at the roof of my mouth.
Have you taken any antibiotics already, or any other medicines? And any allergies?
model.why: Checks for prior amoxicillin and allergies

model.text: Just paracetamol. No allergies.
How are you managing with eating, drinking and your course? Anyone around to help if you get worse?
There are people around at uni. Missing lectures is stressing me out.
What do you think is going on, and what worries you most?
Tonsillitis, I reckon. I just need to be fit for Saturday. It’s a big one.
So it’s the match and falling behind with lectures. That makes sense. Let me tell you what I think.

I think this is most likely glandular fever rather than ordinary tonsillitis. The week-plus of sore throat, the fevers, the glands at the back of your neck and being this exhausted fit it well. It’s caused by a virus, so antibiotics won’t help. One of the common ones, amoxicillin, gives people with glandular fever a nasty rash, so we specifically avoid it.
model.why: Names glandular fever, explains no antibiotics and the amoxicillin rash

model.text: So no antibiotics at all? My mate got them.

Not for this. If a blood test showed something different we’d rethink, but antibiotics would give you the side-effects without the benefit. What will help is rest, fluids, and regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, plus salty water gargles.
model.why: Resists the request with a clear reason and gives supportive care

model.text: Right. And Saturday?

This is the important bit, and I’m sorry. Glandular fever often swells the spleen, an organ under your left ribs. A swollen spleen can tear with a knock or a tackle, which is rare but can be life-threatening. So no rugby Saturday, no contact sport and no heavy gym lifting for at least four weeks from when this started, and longer if your spleen is still big or you’re still unwell.
model.why: Splenic rupture risk and the sport rule

model.text: That’s gutting. Could I just play half?

I get how frustrating that is. The risk is highest in these first weeks, and it only takes one tackle. I’d rather you miss one match than risk your spleen. When we review, I’ll check your tummy and we’ll decide together when it’s safe to get back to contact, rather than guessing. Many people are back to light training sooner than they fear.
model.why: Empathy while holding the safety line, with a route back

model.text: Okay. What about tests?

I’d like you to come in today or tomorrow for a quick blood test, a blood count, the glandular fever test and liver tests, and I’ll feel your tummy for the spleen at the same time. If the glandular fever test is negative, I may repeat it or do other tests, including an HIV test, which we offer routinely for this kind of illness.
model.why: FBC, Monospot, LFTs, face-to-face spleen check; repeat or HIV test if negative

model.text: Fine. Can you do me a note for uni?

I can explain what the diagnosis is once the test is back. Most universities have their own process for missed work when you’re ill, so let your tutor or student support know now. Pace yourself, as the tiredness can take a few weeks to lift.
model.why: Practical support for his studies with realistic expectations

model.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what are you going to do?
No antibiotics. Paracetamol or ibuprofen, fluids, rest. Blood test and tummy check. No rugby or weights for at least four weeks until you say it’s okay.

Spot on. Call 999 if you get sudden bad pain in the upper left of your tummy or the tip of your left shoulder, or feel faint. Go to A&E if you start drooling, can’t swallow fluids or your breathing gets noisy or hard. Let someone near you know about these signs too. I’ll see you with the results, and again before any return to contact sport.
model.why: Specific safety-net for spleen and airway; planned review and return-to-sport check

social.t: Missed lectures and assessments cause stress. Point him to student support and his university’s process for illness; tell him fatigue may affect study for weeks.
Missing a big match is a real loss for a young sportsman. Acknowledge it and give a clear, reviewed route back.

legal.t: Fit notes relate to fitness for work. For study, universities use their own processes; a GP may provide a factual letter, which can carry a fee.
At 19 he is an adult; results and advice are shared with others, such as coaches or family, only with his consent.

professional.t: Declining an unnecessary antibiotic, with a clear explanation, is good practice under NICE NG84 and avoids harm from amoxicillin in EBV infection.
Video allows a look at the throat and nodes, but the spleen needs a face-to-face check before advising on return to contact sport.

community.t: Student health and wellbeing services; club physiotherapists or coaches for a graded return once cleared at review.

redFlags: Drooling, difficulty swallowing fluids, stridor or breathlessness
Sudden left upper abdominal or left shoulder-tip pain, faintness
Persistent or enlarging nodes, night sweats or weight loss

Who is around to notice if he deteriorates
ice: Concern: missing Saturday’s match and falling behind

playbook.diagnosis: “This is most likely glandular fever, a viral infection. Antibiotics won’t help, and the main risk to manage is your spleen.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The glandular fever virus makes your immune system work overtime. Your glands, tonsils and often your spleen swell up while it fights. The spleen sits just under your left ribs, and while it’s swollen, a hard knock can tear it.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for antibiotics to make Saturday. I know that’s not the answer you wanted, but missing one match protects you from a rare but serious injury.”
management.psychosocial: Validate the loss of the match; give a reviewed route back to rugby; help with university processes; share the warning signs with people around him, with his agreement.
sharedPlan: FBC, Monospot and LFTs with a face-to-face spleen check; repeat or EBV serology and HIV test if negative
No antibiotics; avoid amoxicillin; paracetamol or ibuprofen (dose per BNF), fluids, gargles
No contact sport or heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks and until reviewed
safetyNet: Sudden left upper abdominal or shoulder-tip pain, faintness: 999
Drooling, cannot swallow fluids, noisy or difficult breathing: A&E
Review with results and before return to contact sport; persistent nodes or weight loss: reassess

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you give the spleen advice to a young rugby player who wants antibiotics. Many candidates recognise glandular fever but forget the sport rule, or prescribe amoxicillin under pressure.

items.fail: Prescribing amoxicillin or another antibiotic to satisfy the request.
items.why: EBV is viral; amoxicillin causes a florid rash; the SPC advises avoiding it when glandular fever is suspected.
items.fix: Explain the virus and the rash, and offer effective symptom relief.

items.why: Splenic rupture is rare but most cases occur in the first 3 to 4 weeks.
items.fix: No contact sport or heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks, and until reviewed.

items.fail: Taking a negative Monospot as the final answer.
items.why: The heterophile test can be negative early and misses some cases (Ebell, JAMA 2016).
items.fix: Repeat or request EBV serology, and offer an HIV test (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020).

items.fail: Never checking the airway or the spleen.
items.why: Airway obstruction and splenic enlargement are the dangerous complications.
items.fix: Ask about drooling and breathing first; arrange a face-to-face abdominal check.

items.fail: Flatly refusing antibiotics and rugby with no empathy.
items.why: He leaves feeling dismissed and may ignore the safety advice.
items.fix: Name the loss of the match, explain the reason and give a route back.

items.why: Splenic rupture needs 999, and the patient must recognise it.
items.fix: “Sudden pain under your left ribs or in your left shoulder tip, or feeling faint: call 999.”

SCA_MODELS.text: Fine. Can you do me a note for uni?

I can explain what the diagnosis is once the test is back. Most universities have their own process for missed work when you’re ill, so let your tutor or student support know now. Pace yourself, as the tiredness can take a few weeks to lift.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical support for his studies with realistic expectations

SCA_MODELS.text: Just so I know I’ve explained it well, what are you going to do?
No antibiotics. Paracetamol or ibuprofen, fluids, rest. Blood test and tummy check. No rugby or weights for at least four weeks until you say it’s okay.

Spot on. Call 999 if you get sudden bad pain in the upper left of your tummy or the tip of your left shoulder, or feel faint. Go to A&E if you start drooling, can’t swallow fluids or your breathing gets noisy or hard. Let someone near you know about these signs too. I’ll see you with the results, and again before any return to contact sport.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net for spleen and airway; planned review and return-to-sport check

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG84 Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2018) · [2] Amoxicillin summary of product characteristics, section 4.4 (avoid if infectious mononucleosis suspected) · [3] Ebell MH et al. JAMA 2016 (diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis) · [4] Sylvester JE et al. Am Fam Physician 2023 (infectious mononucleosis: rapid evidence review) · [5] BHIVA/BASHH/BIA Adult HIV testing guidelines (2020) · [7] NICE NG206 ME/CFS (2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A young adult with more than a week of severe sore throat, fever, marked fatigue and posterior as well as anterior neck nodes most likely has glandular fever (EBV). Confirm with FBC and film and EBV serology (or a heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, per the local laboratory pathway), with LFTs if clinically indicated. It is viral: antibiotics will not help, and amoxicillin causes a florid rash. The key safety message is the spleen: no contact sport or heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks and until reviewed, so no rugby on Saturday. Safety-net for airway obstruction and splenic rupture.

points.t: Prolonged sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate, marked fatigue, and tender posterior cervical nodes are typical of infectious mononucleosis in teenagers and young adults. Palatal petechiae, splenomegaly and mild hepatitis support it. Ebell (JAMA 2016) [3]: posterior cervical, axillary or inguinal nodes, palatal petechiae and splenomegaly make it more likely.

FBC and film (lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes), and EBV-specific serology as the preferred confirmatory test per the local laboratory pathway; LFTs if jaundice, hepatomegaly or marked systemic illness. A heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, where used, is about 87% sensitive and 91% specific and is unreliable in the first week [3], so a negative result does not exclude EBV when suspicion remains. If negative with a mononucleosis-like illness, offer an HIV test: BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020 [5] lists mononucleosis-like syndrome as an indicator condition.

EBV is viral and antibiotics do not shorten it. Amoxicillin (and ampicillin) cause a widespread maculopapular rash in most people with glandular fever; the SPC [2] advises avoiding it when infectious mononucleosis is suspected. If a separate bacterial tonsillitis needed treating, NICE NG84 [1] first choice is phenoxymethylpenicillin for 5 to 10 days (dose per BNF).

Rest as needed, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever (dose per BNF), saltwater gargles. Avoid alcohol while unwell and until liver tests settle. Most people feel better within 2 to 4 weeks, but tiredness can last longer.

Splenic rupture is rare (often quoted as about 0.1 to 0.5%, though exact estimates are uncertain) but potentially fatal; most reported cases occur in the first month, although late rupture can occur [4]. Advise no contact or collision sport and no heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks from the start of symptoms, and longer while the spleen is enlarged or he is unwell. Agree the return at review, not by guesswork.

Airway: drooling, inability to swallow fluids, noisy breathing or breathlessness → emergency. Splenic rupture: sudden severe left upper abdominal pain, left shoulder-tip pain, faintness → 999. Also severe dehydration, jaundice or bleeding.

Persistent or enlarging nodes, night sweats, weight loss or splenomegaly without explanation need reassessment: [6] lymphoma criteria. Fatigue beyond 6 weeks with post-exertional symptoms: consider ME/CFS assessment per NICE NG206 [7].

social.t: Missed lectures and assessments cause stress. Point him to student support and his university’s process for illness; tell him fatigue may affect study for weeks.
Missing a big match is a real loss for a young sportsman. Acknowledge it and give a clear, reviewed route back.

At 19 he is an adult; results and advice are shared with others, such as coaches or family, only with his consent.

professional.t: Declining an unnecessary antibiotic, with a clear explanation, is good practice under NICE NG84 and avoids harm from amoxicillin in EBV infection.
Video allows a look at the throat and nodes, but the spleen needs a face-to-face check before advising on return to contact sport.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is most likely glandular fever, a viral infection. Antibiotics won’t help, and the main risk to manage is your spleen.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The glandular fever virus makes your immune system work overtime. Your glands, tonsils and often your spleen swell up while it fights. The spleen sits just under your left ribs, and while it’s swollen, a hard knock can tear it.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for antibiotics to make Saturday. I know that’s not the answer you wanted, but missing one match protects you from a rare but serious injury.”

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you give the spleen advice to a young rugby player who wants antibiotics. Many candidates recognise glandular fever but forget the sport rule, or prescribe amoxicillin under pressure.

items.fail: Prescribing amoxicillin or another antibiotic to satisfy the request.
items.why: EBV is viral; amoxicillin causes a florid rash; the SPC advises avoiding it when glandular fever is suspected.
items.fix: Explain the virus and the rash, and offer effective symptom relief.

items.why: Splenic rupture is rare but most cases occur in the first 3 to 4 weeks.
items.fix: No contact sport or heavy lifting for at least 4 weeks, and until reviewed.

items.fail: Taking a negative Monospot as the final answer.
items.why: The heterophile test can be negative early and misses some cases (Ebell, JAMA 2016).
items.fix: Repeat or request EBV serology, and offer an HIV test (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020).

items.fail: Never checking the airway or the spleen.
items.why: Airway obstruction and splenic enlargement are the dangerous complications.
items.fix: Ask about drooling and breathing first; arrange a face-to-face abdominal check.

items.fail: Flatly refusing antibiotics and rugby with no empathy.
items.why: He leaves feeling dismissed and may ignore the safety advice.
items.fix: Name the loss of the match, explain the reason and give a route back.

items.why: Splenic rupture needs 999, and the patient must recognise it.
items.fix: “Sudden pain under your left ribs or in your left shoulder tip, or feeling faint: call 999.”
